gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the makers' refill claims on the same basis. Every claim assumes the station's full solar input. Anker's own spec splits the C1000 Gen 2 input into two bands: 11–28 V at 8.2 A (about 230 W at most) and 29–60 V at 14.5 A. So two low-voltage panels wired in parallel get well under half of the 600 W behind its '1.8 hours' figure. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 claims the same 70-minute full refill as the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. The difference is that the BLUETTI takes its 1,000 W through one 12–60 V, 20 A input, while EcoFlow splits its 1,000 W across two 500 W inputs.
standout_why: I could not open the rival pages this time. The REI-hosted DELTA 3 Plus manual returned 403, and solargenreview.com and several maker pages returned 429. This judgement is therefore based on what ChatGPT showed the shopper and on the maker pages I did open. ChatGPT's answers repeat the headline figures: EcoFlow's '70 minutes' and Anker's '1.8-hour refill at maximum solar input'. They give no input voltage or current conditions, do not split two panels in series from two in parallel, and never mention the Elite 100 V2. Our current page already contrasts two inputs with one and gives voltage windows. It does not have Anker's 230 W low-voltage cap, the matching 70-minute claims from EcoFlow and BLUETTI, or the average watts each claim implies.
decides: This mostly confirms the DELTA 3 Plus pick for 'two panels', because it takes one panel per input and two panels need no series or parallel wiring. The Elite 100 V2 makes the same 70-minute claim for $499, but only when both panels are wired into one string that sits between 50 V working and 60 V open-circuit. Wired in parallel, it is capped at 20 A times the panels' working voltage. On the Anker C1000 Gen 2, the '1.8 hours' needs a string above 41 V. Two small panels in parallel at about 18–20 V stay inside the 8.2 A band and reach only about a third of that rate.

findings.label: Two 400 W rigid panels on the single input
findings.value: Cannot be used: in series they exceed the 500 W limit, and in parallel they exceed the 15 A limit (input is 11–60 V, 15 A, 500 W)
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus | EcoFlow Product FAQs | EcoFlow US
findings.note: This is EcoFlow's own worked example. It says the panels' open-circuit voltage, current and power must all fall within the input's limits, and if any one is exceeded 'the solar panels cannot be used'. The same page says the DELTA 3 'with a 500W MPPT recharges in 2 hours'.

findings.value: 1,000 W max, 12–60 V, 20 A max; 'Full in 70 Minutes'

findings.note: No footnote or conditions are given for the 70-minute claim. This is the same headline as the DELTA 3 Plus, through one input range. Arithmetic: 1,000 W ÷ 20 A means the string must work at 50 V or more, and open-circuit voltage must stay at 60 V or below. Two panels in parallel are capped at 20 A × their working voltage.

findings.label: Solar input bands
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station - 1,024Wh | 2,000W - Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Arithmetic: 28 V × 8.2 A = about 230 W at most in the low band. Reaching 600 W at 14.5 A needs about 41.4 V or more. Two ~18–20 V panels wired in parallel stay in the low band (230 W or less). Wiring them in series moves the string into the high band.

findings.label: Refill claim
findings.value: 'Plug in 600W (60V max) of solar and recharge fully in just 1.8 hours'
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station - 1,024Wh | 2,000W - Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: No footnote gives a charge range or the panel used. Normalised: 1,024 Wh ÷ 1.8 h = an average of about 569 W into the battery (95% of 600 W). At the 230 W low-band cap, the same 1,024 Wh would take about 4.5 h before conversion losses (1,024 ÷ 230).
